title: Task Graphs — Dependencies and the Frontier

questions.prompt: Graph: schema → api, schema → migration, api → tests, and migration → deploy, tests → deploy. Everything unfinished. What is the frontier, and what is it after the schema finishes?
options: Now: schema. After: api and migration
Now: api, migration, tests, deploy. After: tests and deploy
Now: schema. After: api, migration, deploy
Now: schema and api. After: migration
questions.explanation: Only schema has no parents, so the frontier starts as just schema. When it finishes, api and migration both have all parents done, so both enter the frontier together. Option B swaps the list for the frontier — unwritten nodes are not runnable, and deploy still needs tests. Option C adds deploy early, but deploy's parent tests has not run. Option D wrongly includes api before schema is done.

questions.prompt: Every node in a wave diagram takes one unit of time, so wave 2 shows api and migration running together. In the real run, migration finishes in seconds but api takes an hour, and migration's child becomes ready. A runner waits for all of wave 2 before starting wave 3. What did it get wrong?
options: Nothing — waves are the frontier by definition
It treated a static wave as a live frontier, so a node that became ready early waited for a slow sibling
It should have put migration in a later wave
It needed to increase the number of waves
questions.explanation: Waves assume equal cost; the frontier is recomputed after every completion, so migration's child can start while api still runs. Option A is the tempting conflation — this lesson exists because waves are not the frontier. Option C would not help; migration genuinely only depends on schema. Option D treats a scheduling strategy as a graph property.

questions.prompt: A run reports "finished" but the `docs` node never executed. `docs` needs `api`, and `api` is in a cycle with `tests`. What kind of node is `docs`, and what should the runner have shown?
options: A sink node; nothing needed to be shown
A stranded node — its parent can never complete, so it never enters the frontier and the run must report it as not-run
A ready node the runner simply skipped
An entry node that was mislabelled
questions.explanation: Because api sits in a cycle it can never finish, so docs never becomes ready; that is a stranded node, and a runner that silently omits it is losing work. Option A is wrong — sink means no outgoing edges, not no execution. Option C is tempting but docs was never ready, because its parent never completed. Option D inverts the definition: an entry node has no parents.

questions.prompt: A teammate says "the critical path is the longest task, so I'll find my slowest node and shorten it." What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing — speed up the slowest node and the project gets faster
The critical path is the longest *chain of dependencies*, not the longest single node; shortening an off-path node changes nothing
The critical path is the shortest path, so they should shorten the fastest task
Critical path is computed from durations only, never from edges
questions.explanation: Critical path length in waves counts sequential *edges*, and the longest chain can run through several medium nodes rather than one slow one. Option A is the tempting rule of thumb and it frequently misfires: a slow node on a short side branch is not on the critical path. Option C reverses longest and shortest. Option D ignores that the chain is defined by edges.
